Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Gemini 4 Argon, and hy4-flash via OpenCode used for the binary reverse engineering, empirical cache probing, and keep-alive tooling. Greetings! If you use Google Antigravity ( agy ) with the big frontier models, you have probably noticed how fast your weekly quota disappears during normal coding sessions [1, 4]. My suspicion was simple: a short prompt-cache lifetime . When you are coding with an agent, you don’t send messages every 10 seconds. You wait for a response, read the diff, run a test, think for 5 minutes, and then send your next prompt. If the prompt cache expires during that 5-minute pause, your next message has to re-ingest the entire conversation history at full price. Instead of just assuming that was true, I decided to actually test it and look inside the Antigravity binaries to see how caching works under the hood. What started as a quick TTL check turned into disassembling a 193 MB Go binary, discovering a dormant keep-alive engine that Google already wrote, binary-searching the exact eviction cliff down to a 15-second window, testing whether /btw side-questions can keep the cache warm, and finally unlocking Google’s built-in zero-trajectory keep-alive engine on a live 6-minute run. To understand why pauses matter, let’s look at how Gemini models handle context in Antigravity. Every turn in an agentic coding session carries a massive prefix: the system prompt, tool schemas, connected MCP servers, skill definitions, and all previous turns. On Gemini 4 models, Antigravity relies exclusively on implicit caching [2, 3]. Unlike explicit caching (where you manually place cache breakpoints and pay for a guaranteed storage lease), implicit caching is an automatic, best-effort prefix match on Google’s backend. When your request hits the implicit cache, cached tokens ( cache_read_tokens ) get a 90% discount compared to regular uncached input_tokens [2]. When the cache misses, you pay 100% on the entire prefix. Google does not publish a fixed TTL for implicit caching. If that TTL is shorter than a typical code-review pause, interactive coding turns into a worst-case workload. Before running live probes, I inspected the local Antigravity installation on macOS ( arm64 ): the desktop app ( /Applications/Antigravity.app , v2.33.0 ), its core Go agent binary ( language_server ), and the standalone CLI ( ~/.gemini/bin/agy , v1.5.11 / 1.5.12 ) across isolated CLI runs. Inspecting the Go symbol table in language_server immediately confirmed that Antigravity tracks cumulative context through CumulativePromptHandler and buckets turn gaps into two telemetry categories: lt_5m (less than 5 minutes) and ge_5m (5 minutes or more). That alone was a strong clue that 5 minutes is the magic number. Digging deeper, I found a file path in the binary’s symbol table: modelapiccpa/keepalive.go . Disassembling its functions ( keepAlivePings , beforeRequest , scheduleNextPingLocked , ping , and trimLastBlock ) revealed that Google already built an automatic background prompt-cache keep-alive mechanism. Here is how their internal keep-alive works: Why do we still lose the cache every 5 minutes? Two gates in the binary stop it from running: Since account-level quota percentages are noisy (other background agents share the same quota pool), I used cache_read_tokens from agy --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json as the primary ground-truth signal. At the end of every turn, agy emits a DONE event for agent_response with three numbers: For the baseline TTL tests, I used gemini-4-hydrogen-low with --effort low and the prompt "Reply with only OK." so output tokens stayed tiny (5 to 25 tokens). To run multi-turn conversations inside a single long-lived process (matching how the desktop app’s language_server runs), I fed NDJSON user events into agy through a persistent FIFO pipe. First, I tried running two separate one-shot agy -p --conversation <same-id> commands back-to-back: Two things stood out immediately: Next, I tested an 8-minute idle gap with no activity, and compared it against an 8-minute window with a single keep-alive ping at +4 minutes : This proved two things: To find the exact cliff where the cache dies, I ran a binary search across idle intervals: The boundary is between 4 min 45 s and 5 min 00 s . That matches both my initial 5-minute estimate and the 4 min 45 s ( 285s ) staleness cutoff hardcoded inside Google’s keepalive.go . Since Gemini gives a 90% discount on cached tokens [2], I calculated the effective token cost ( C ) of any turn by weighting cache_read_tokens at 0.1x : $$C = T_{\text{uncached}} + 0.1 \times T_{\text{cached}}$$ In my measured 8-minute test window: Even on an empty conversation with just the 14.8k base prefix, one well-timed ping saves 9,653 to 13,286 effective tokens ( 29-36% savings ), a 3.7x return on the cost of the ping. My test conversation had almost zero history ( ~14.8k cached prefix). In a real coding session where you have read several files and built up a 150,000-token context ( ~147,850 cached prefix + ~2,150 uncached tail), the numbers scale quickly: In a 150k-token session, pausing for 5 minutes to read a diff, read a response, or grab a coffee costs you 133,065 extra effective tokens on your very next message. Keep-alive is cheaper than a miss, not free. If you walk away from your desk for two hours and let a script ping every 4 minutes, you will burn far more tokens pinging than if you just let the cache expire once. The maximum number of consecutive idle pings ( N_max ) before keep-alive costs more than a single cold miss ( C_cold - C_warm = 0.9 * T_cached ) is: $$N_{\text{max}} = \left\lfloor \frac{0.9 \times T_{\text{cached}}}{T_{\text{uncached}} + 0.1 \times T_{\text{cached}}} \right\rfloor$$ This is why Google’s internal keepalive.go tracks a prompt_cache_keep_alive_max_pings budget per conversation. Sending a normal user message as a keep-alive in the CLI has one downside: each ping adds a user and assistant turn to your trajectory. Antigravity has a /btw slash command that lets you ask a side question in a forked thread without adding anything to the main conversation history. I tested whether /btw could act as a clean keep-alive. Because /btw is blocked in print and stream mode, I drove the interactive TUI through a pseudo-terminal ( pty ) and read the resulting token counts from transcript.jsonl : Here is what happened in the trace: Disassembling setSideQuestionPromptSection and newSideQuestionBoundaryStep in agy explains why: /btw creates a brand-new child conversation ID ( cascade_id ) and injects side-question instructions (~873 extra tokens). Because the child fork has a different conversation ID, its own call misses the cache and pays full price, which simultaneously refreshes the shared 14,770-token base prefix in the backend cache for the parent conversation. So /btw works, but it is the most expensive option: it costs ~4.9x a normal warm ping and ~26% more than just accepting a cache miss . To get both the low token cost of a normal warm ping and the zero trajectory pollution of /btw , I looked back at the dormant internal engine from Section 2.2. Google’s engineers already wrote that exact logic inside modelapiccpa/keepalive.go ( trimLastBlock + max_output_tokens = 1 , scheduled at 4m 30s with a 4m 45s staleness cutoff). It was just gated off by two checks in the agy binary: To test whether Google’s internal engine works end-to-end on Gemini once unlocked, I built a verification and binary-patching script: I ran a live 6-minute trial on the patched agy binary using gemini-3.8-flash-low ( --effort low , prompt "Reply with only OK." ), sending only two user messages 6 minutes 6 seconds apart , past the 4m 45s-5m 00s eviction cliff. First, I ran a fast 20-second smoke test on a temporary binary copy with the internal timer patched to 15s ( --interval-sec 15 --staleness-sec 45 ), which confirmed that the background streamGenerateContent ping fired automatically at +17s and Turn 2 hit the cache ( 11,835 cached tokens). Then I ran the full 6-minute test using Google’s stock 270s ( 4m 30s ) timer: Checking the CLI’s HTTP trace log ( http_helpers.go ) and the conversation’s transcript.jsonl ( b476755e-baa4-451f-913a-e70cfb0bc892 ) confirmed all three signals simultaneously: Here is what I learned from putting Antigravity under the microscope: Caveats worth keeping in mind: my effective token math uses Gemini’s published 90% implicit-cache discount [2] (internal subscription quota weights may vary slightly), and implicit caching is best-effort, so backend TTLs can shift under load.
